topic: Design a skill for better Markdown document writing and plan a follow-up research session
initialPrompt:
I want to create a skill for my agents, that helps them write better md documents. And i wanna do a research session next session that we will use to make out md document writing skills good, and look also for some potential md document creation skills we can add to our stack. I want you to grill me to help me lay out exactly what my plan is.

Activate your karpathy and write a skillv2 skills. Don't worry about activating any other skills thats all you need.

qAndA.question: Self-resolved decision: This session will only clarify the design and define the next-session research brief; it will not perform the research, create the Markdown-writing skill, or add other skills. (The user may veto this boundary.)

What is the primary job you want the new Markdown-document skill to perform: (A) act as a universal Markdown writing-quality layer that can improve or validate any Markdown document, (B) create specific document types from structured inputs, such as nav guides, CONTEXT/PLAN docs, ADRs, system-design docs, and handoffs, or (C) route to and coordinate several narrower document-creation skills? My recommendation is **(C) as the eventual architecture, but with one narrowly scoped first skill** whose job is to improve the quality of an already-selected Markdown document type—not to own every document type or replace the existing specialized skills. Which direction matches your actual plan?
qAndA.answer: a. mainly will be for like creating personal notes/guides for myself. like for example my video guide. My agent did research about how to make good videos,and found some fiormulas/frameworks people use, and made me a step by step guide for my own videos. or just quick temp documents.  I want research backed data behind this skill, to make the documents efficient for human readers. the psychology behin what makes a good md document. What other people are currently using aswell that I could adopt and add on to my stack.

qAndA.question: Revision to the earlier recommendation: The first skill should be a universal Markdown document-writing layer for personal notes, guides, and quick temporary documents. Its core audience is the user as a human reader, and its guidance should be grounded in research on comprehension, information retrieval, memory, scanning, and usable document structure. It should not initially be a router or a replacement for specialized document skills. (Self-resolved from your answer — user may veto.)

Should the skill primarily (A) generate a new personal Markdown note or guide from the user’s goal, source material, or research findings, (B) review and improve an existing Markdown document, or (C) do both as equal first-class workflows? My recommendation is **(C), with generation as the default path and review as a short, explicit second path**: the skill should help an agent turn research into an efficient human-readable guide, then optionally audit the draft for clarity, scanability, evidence traceability, and unnecessary complexity. Which scope do you want for version one?

Self-resolved decision: Version one will prioritize generating new personal Markdown notes and guides. Existing-document review is out of scope for the first version, except for any lightweight self-check the skill performs on the document it just generated. (The user may veto this decision.)

When the agent uses this skill to create a personal note or guide, what should the normal output workflow be: (A) write the Markdown file directly after gathering enough context, (B) show a draft in chat and wait for approval before writing, or (C) use a lightweight adaptive rule—write directly for quick temporary notes, but show a draft and request approval for substantial or research-heavy guides? My recommendation is **(C)** because a video-framework guide benefits from review, while a throwaway temp note should not incur a ceremony. Should the skill also choose the filename and destination automatically from your project conventions, or ask you when they are ambiguous?
qAndA.answer: I updted the grill skill, you can reformat the questions now  (check the skill)\n\nMy asnwer for this question though is we can figure this out after the research in next session.

qAndA.question: Self-resolved decision: Defer the output ceremony, filename rules, and destination rules until the next research session. That research should first identify what workflow best supports quick temporary notes versus substantial personal guides; this grill will not force those choices prematurely. (The user may veto this decision.)

If the research finds a conflict between evidence-backed principles about human comprehension and popular documentation practices that people currently use, which should govern the skill by default? My recommendation is: evidence-backed principles govern the core rules; current practices are included as optional patterns only when they have a clear usability benefit and do not add ceremony or visual clutter. Do you agree with that priority?

Self-resolved decision: Evidence-backed findings about human comprehension, information retrieval, memory, scanning, and usable document structure will govern the core Markdown-writing skill. Current practices and other people’s approaches will be researched as optional patterns or candidates for adoption, not as equal authority when they conflict with stronger evidence. (The user may veto this decision.)

What should the next research session treat as the primary success outcome: (A) produce a research-backed writing rubric/checklist that the future skill can apply while generating personal notes and guides, (B) identify and rank additional Markdown/document-creation skills or reusable patterns to add to your stack, or (C) produce both, with the evidence-backed writing rubric as the core deliverable and the skill/pattern inventory as a secondary adoption backlog? My recommendation is **(C)**, because the inventory is useful only if it is evaluated against the core human-reader criteria rather than collected as a disconnected list. Is that the right priority?
qAndA.answer: Success would be valuable information about how to make psychologically efficient and pretty md documents, aswell as finding useful md document skills that are already made and used by people that I could add to my stack.

qAndA.question: Self-resolved decision: The next research session has two co-equal value streams: (1) evidence-backed guidance for making Markdown documents psychologically efficient, readable, and visually appealing; and (2) discovery and evaluation of existing Markdown/document-creation skills or reusable patterns that could be added to the stack. The research output should connect the two streams by judging discovered skills against the human-reader criteria, rather than treating the skill inventory as a standalone list. (The user may veto this decision.)

For the phrase “pretty Markdown documents,” what should the research optimize for? My recommendation is **functional visual polish**: strong hierarchy, whitespace, typography, restrained color/callouts, useful tables or diagrams, and fast scanning—while avoiding decoration that increases cognitive load, maintenance burden, or rendering fragility. Should “pretty” mean this kind of usable visual design, or are there stronger aesthetic goals you want the research to pursue?

Self-resolved decision: The research should optimize for Markdown documents that are both psychologically efficient and distinctly pretty. “Pretty” is an explicit design goal, not merely an accidental side effect of readability; however, the research should still identify where visual styling improves comprehension versus where it becomes distracting or fragile. (The user may veto this decision.)

Which Markdown rendering environments should the next research session treat as the compatibility baseline? My recommendation is **GitHub and VS Code preview first**, with the skill favoring portable Markdown and treating renderer-specific enhancements as optional. This matches the existing mermaid skill’s GitHub-safe orientation and reduces the risk that attractive formatting breaks elsewhere. Should the research use that baseline, or prioritize another reader such as Obsidian?
qAndA.answer: please make your questions look nice to read, theyre kinda all compact, no formatting. \nvscode preview mainly

qAndA.question: Revision to the prior self-resolved decision: The next research session should optimize for **VS Code Markdown Preview first**. GitHub portability remains a useful secondary constraint where practical, but it is no longer the primary rendering baseline. (The user may veto this revision.)

How should the next research session handle Markdown features that look especially good in VS Code but may not render consistently elsewhere?

**My recommendation:** use a two-tier approach.

- **Core layer:** portable Markdown that remains structurally sound across common renderers.
- **VS Code polish layer:** optional features—such as enhanced callouts, styling conventions, diagrams, or other preview-friendly elements—used when they materially improve the document.

This would let the skill make documents genuinely pretty for your main environment without pretending every renderer supports the same presentation layer. Does that match your plan?
qAndA.answer: we'll figure this out in the next/research session

qAndA.question: Self-resolved decision: Defer the exact boundary between portable Markdown and VS Code-specific polish to the next research session. That session should compare renderer capabilities and decide which visual features belong in the core format versus an optional VS Code enhancement layer. (The user may veto this decision.)

What kinds of existing Markdown/document-creation skills should the next research session search for and evaluate?

My recommendation is to search broadly across four categories, then rank only the candidates that fit your personal-note and guide workflow:

1. **Research-to-guide skills** — turn findings, sources, formulas, or frameworks into actionable personal guides.
2. **Markdown quality and presentation skills** — improve hierarchy, scanability, visual polish, and reader comprehension.
3. **Knowledge-management skills** — create notes, indexes, quick references, summaries, or linked personal documentation.
4. **Markdown tooling skills** — validate, lint, render, convert, or enhance Markdown documents.

Should the research cover all four categories, or should it stay focused on a narrower subset?

Self-resolved decision: The next research session will evaluate all four categories: research-to-guide skills, Markdown quality/presentation skills, knowledge-management skills, and Markdown tooling skills. Candidates will be filtered through the project’s actual use case: personal notes, practical guides, research-derived frameworks, and quick temporary documents. (The user may veto this decision.)

How should the next research session evaluate whether an existing skill or pattern is worth adding to your stack?

My recommendation is to score each candidate against a compact adoption rubric:

- **Reader value:** does it improve comprehension, memory, retrieval, scanning, or visual appeal?
- **Fit:** does it help with personal notes, practical guides, research synthesis, or temporary documents?
- **Evidence quality:** are its principles grounded in credible research or demonstrated practice?
- **Distinct value:** does it add something your current skills do not already provide?
- **Operational cost:** how much ceremony, maintenance, dependency, or context does it introduce?
- **Adoption path:** can it be installed, adapted, or incorporated cleanly into this stack?

Should the research use this kind of explicit ranking rubric, or do you want a looser collection of interesting options?
qAndA.answer: we'll figure it out in the next research session, but this may be a good start.

qAndA.question: Self-resolved decision: Use the proposed adoption rubric as a starting hypothesis for the next research session, not as a locked scoring system. The research may refine, replace, or simplify the rubric after examining real candidate skills and evidence. (The user may veto this decision.)

What should the next research session produce for the future skill authoring step?

My recommendation is a research package with four parts:

1. **Evidence base** — findings about comprehension, memory, information retrieval, visual hierarchy, aesthetics, and cognitive load, with source quality clearly separated.
2. **Practical design principles** — concise rules for creating psychologically efficient and pretty Markdown notes and guides.
3. **Worked examples** — before/after transformations or model document patterns, ideally shaped around your real use cases such as a research-derived video guide.
4. **Adoption candidates** — existing skills and tools across the four agreed categories, ranked with rationale, overlap analysis, and a recommended adopt/adapt/reject outcome.

Is this the right shape for the research deliverable, or is there something essential you want added or removed?
qAndA.answer: This is a good baseline/start yes.

qAndA.question: Self-resolved decision: Treat the four-part research package—evidence base, practical design principles, worked examples, and adoption candidates—as the initial deliverable shape for the next session. The researchers may extend it if the evidence reveals a necessary additional section, but they should avoid adding sections merely for completeness. (The user may veto this decision.)

The decision tree is now exhausted. How do you want to close?

- **(a) Close and hand off** — close the session log, then—with your go-ahead—the `handoff` skill can write a Markdown handoff document for the next research session.
- **(b) Close without handoff** — close the session log; no handoff document.
- **(c) Leave it active** — keep the session log open so you can resume later.

summary:
The session defined the initial plan for a future Markdown-document-writing skill and its preceding research session. The skill should primarily generate personal Markdown notes and practical guides—especially research-derived guides such as a personal video-making framework—and may also support quick temporary documents. Its core purpose is to make documents psychologically efficient and distinctly pretty for human readers, using evidence-based findings about comprehension, memory, information retrieval, scanning, visual hierarchy, aesthetics, and cognitive load. Evidence should govern the core rules; popular documentation practices should be treated as optional patterns unless supported by usability value.

The next research session should investigate four categories of existing skills and tools: research-to-guide skills, Markdown quality and presentation skills, knowledge-management skills, and Markdown tooling skills. Its baseline deliverable should include an evidence base, practical design principles, worked examples, and adoption candidates with overlap analysis and adopt/adapt/reject recommendations. The proposed candidate-evaluation rubric is only a starting hypothesis and may be refined during research. The research should prioritize VS Code Markdown Preview, while deferring the exact boundary between portable Markdown and VS Code-specific polish until that session. Output ceremony, filename, destination, and whether/how to review drafts should also be decided after research. No skill implementation or research was performed during this grilling session.
